name: Self-inductance
description: A metal ring alone in your solenoid, whose field swings with a fixed amplitude, $B = B_0 \sin \omega t$: your supply sets only how fast. The changing field drives a current round the ring (Faraday's law), and that current makes a field of its own, against the change (Lenz's law): the ring is a one-turn coil, an inductance $L$ in series with its resistance $R$. While $\omega L/R$ is small the heat grows as $\omega^2$; past $\omega L/R \approx 1$ the ring's own field cancels the drive's in its hole and the heat levels off. Set $\omega$ so that the ring takes between 1000 and 1500 of heat per unit time (averaged from $t = 2.5$ to $10$).

reality.represents: A closed metal ring's self-inductance: a shorted turn in a swinging field

remarks.detail: The ring's current makes a field against the change of the drive's flux through it. Past ωL/R ≈ 1 its own field cancels the drive's in the hole and the current, held by L, no longer grows: the heat levels off, as an inductor's reactance limits its current.
At the highest frequencies the current crowds to the ring's outer face and the heat grows only as √ω.

The model's speed of light is slow, so that the ring bends at a playable frequency: there c/ω is about the ring's size. A real ring that large would radiate and its field would lag; the model leaves both out (the Darwin limit). A copper ring 2 cm across bends near 6 kHz, where c/ω is 8 km.

The carriers are thirty times denser than the other levels' metals (ω_p τ ≈ 5, a heavily doped semiconductor's; copper's is ~250), so that the ring's inductance outweighs its resistance at a frequency the model can follow.

Carriers bounce off randomly placed hard discs and leave with a fresh thermal speed; the lattice takes the heat and never warms. Real carriers scatter off lattice vibrations and impurities at rates that depend on energy and temperature.

The strip is infinitely long along z, its carriers lines of charge moving as one: currents are per unit length, and the noise is larger than a real conductor's, whose carriers move independently along its length.

electrodes.label: inert electrode (floating, emits nothing; the model needs one)
